# Will It Stick?: full page text

> Complete text of willitstick.app: the homepage, the Examples page,
> the Starters page, the Privacy page, and the Terms page, plus the
> guides, the Method page, Ways to say it, and the question pages.
> Will It Stick? is a free tool in plain words. Paste words you need to land, plus one
> line on what they should do. Cold readers test three transformations of your words and
> hand back the version that sticks, the winner first with your original alongside;
> underneath, the check scores your words and hands back the core they heard, small
> starter shapes, one fix, and four plain grades out of 5 last, with the six-score diagnosis one tap below them. Both tools ask a short question
> round first when the readers hit a gap only you can fill. It names one fix and, when
> a check passes, shows it applied to your words. Nothing sends itself; what goes out
> is your call. Your words are not recorded or kept; only a daily count of runs is kept. The site is an early preview.
> Text captured from the site source, 2026-11-03. The live pages are the record.

## Homepage (https://willitstick.app/)

Paste words you're about to send.
Get back the version that sticks.

Quick-start moments: What's new with me · Recommend something · A story I tell · Say thanks · Ask or invite · A hard message.

Your words (paste a note, a toast, a post, a hard message, or drop a .txt or .md file).
What should your words do? (One line: who reads them, and what should they do, feel, or remember?)
Button: Check if it sticks.
Your words are not recorded or kept; only a daily count of checks is kept.
Try a sample: A repair night note · A work memo.

Three real checks (from real panel runs; the full runs are on the Examples page). A work note that hid the risk: Before: "Status update: The project is progressing. Several workstreams are underway and we are addressing various issues as they arise. Stakeholders have been engaged. We expect continued progress in the coming period and will provide further updates as things develop." After: "Status update: The project is at risk of delay. Several workstreams are underway and we are addressing various issues as they arise. Stakeholders have been engaged. We expect continued progress in the coming period and will provide further updates as things develop." The line the readers kept named the risk her goal named: "The project is at risk." The note itself never said it, and every score was 1 or 2 of 10. 1 line changed. The rest stayed the same. The fix asked for one more line, 'I need your help this week.' The rewrite never added it. A hard text to a friend: the text never says what happened last weekend. Readers kept "Friend hurt last weekend." Feeling scored 7 of 10; the scene scored 4. The one fix: "Say what happened last weekend to show why you want to talk." A toast with no one scene: all three readers kept "Thanks to all for being here," and not one kept a thing about Sarah. Stories scored 1 of 10. The one fix: "Name one thing Sarah did that was great. Cut the rest."

A result shows, in this order: what they'll hear (one quoted line, or the plain split when readers heard three different points), with each reader's own heard line under it; other ways to say it (seven versions of the same words, each read cold and ranked, strongest first in the result and the rest one tap away; when the readers hit a gap only you can fill, they ask two or three questions, one at a time, your answers run a second set, and the result shows what changed); the one fix; before and after (your words as pasted beside your words with only the one fix applied, changed words marked, with a count of lines changed; when the server-side limit drops the after view, the one fix stands as a tip only); starters beside the after card (the proverb, start with a question, the story, words you can picture), labeled "Shapes to start from. Not your text."; and four plain grades out of 5 last, in a compact strip (Easy to read, Holds your attention, The point lands, You'd pass it on, each graded directly by the three cold readers in the same read), with the six-score diagnosis one tap down (Simple, Unexpected, Concrete, Credible, Emotional, Stories, each the mid score of three cold readers, the weakest named, the full scores with a one-line reason and the spread). Every result ends: "One fix, shown applied to your words when it passes. Nothing is sent anywhere; what goes out is your call."

### How it works

1. Three cold readers score your words. They never see each other's notes.
2. You get what they'll hear first, then other ways to say it. If the readers hit a gap only
you can fill, they ask, and your answers sharpen a second set.
3. One fix, shown on your words. Four plain grades out of 5 sit last; the six-score diagnosis is one tap below them. You decide
what to send.

### Method and sources

The SUCCESs checklist comes from Made to Stick, by Chip Heath and Dan Heath, backed by Tversky and Shafir (1992), Loewenstein (1994), and Paivio (1971).
We test this tool against plain AI: the same ten messages, the same six-part rubric for both sides, judged blind. Across three runs the panel won 7, 5, and 7 of 10.
Read the full method: the baseline, the judges, and every run. (https://willitstick.app/method)
This tool is independent. The authors and the publisher did not endorse it, and we have no tie to them.

## Examples (https://willitstick.app/examples)

Six real checks. Real runs. Sample words. No fake wins.
Every text is a sample; every run is real. Three cold readers scored each text without seeing each other's notes. Scores are the middle of three. Words in quotes are the run's own words.

### A repair night note (chip: Ask or invite; the site's own sample)

Words: "Your toaster died on a Tuesday. The shop wants $90 to look at it. We fix it free. Every first Saturday, neighbors bring broken lamps, bikes, and toasters to the Maple Street hall. Last month we fixed 63 things and threw away none of them. Bring one broken thing. Leave with it working, plus a cup of coffee."
Goal: "Get neighbors to come to one repair night."
Core heard: "Fix things free."
Scores: Simple 8, Unexpected 6, Concrete 9, Credible 7, Emotional 5, Stories 8.
One fix: "Add a feeling, like 'fun'."
One starter: Proverb: "Fix it free, save money."

### A work note that hid the risk (sample text; a work note, not one of the six chips; this is also the run pictured when the site is shared)

Words: "Status update: The project is progressing. Several workstreams are underway and we are addressing various issues as they arise. Stakeholders have been engaged. We expect continued progress in the coming period and will provide further updates as things develop."
Goal: "Update my manager so she knows the launch is at risk and what I need from her this week"
Core heard: "The project is at risk."
Scores: Simple 2, Unexpected 1, Concrete 1, Credible 2, Emotional 1, Stories 1.
One fix: "The project is at risk of delay. I need your help this week."
With the one fix: "Status update: The project is at risk of delay. Several workstreams are underway and we are addressing various issues as they arise. Stakeholders have been engaged. We expect continued progress in the coming period and will provide further updates as things develop."
One line changed. The rest is the same text. The fix asked for one more line, 'I need your help this week.' The rewrite never added it.

### A podcast tip with no name (chip: Recommend something; sample text from the test set)

Words: "You should listen to this podcast I found. It is really interesting and the host is great and talks about a lot of different topics. I think you would like it. I listened to a few episodes and they were all good."
Goal: "Recommend a podcast to a close friend so she actually presses play this week"
Core heard: "Listen to this interesting podcast."
Scores: Simple 3, Unexpected 1, Concrete 1, Credible 2, Emotional 2, Stories 1.
One fix: "Cut the vague parts. Just say the podcast's name."
The text names no show, so the rewrite could only drop 'really'. The real fix needs a fact only you can add: the show's name.

### A toast with no scene (chip: Say thanks; sample text from the test set)

Words: "I just want to say thank you to everyone for being here. Sarah is a wonderful person and a great friend to all of us. We are so lucky to know her. Here is to many more years of happiness and good times together."
Goal: "Give a short birthday toast for my friend Sarah that guests will remember tomorrow"
Core heard: "Thanks to all for being here"
Scores: Simple 8, Unexpected 2, Concrete 2, Credible 4, Emotional 5, Stories 1.
One fix: "Name one thing Sarah did that was great. Cut the rest."
One starter: Start with a question: "What makes Sarah special?"

### A hard message to a friend (chip: A hard message; sample text from the test set)

Words: "Hey, I need to talk about something. I have been feeling kind of off about how things went last weekend and I do not want it to be weird. You matter to me and I value our friendship a lot. Can we talk sometime?"
Goal: "Tell a close friend last weekend hurt me and ask to talk, without sounding angry"
Core heard: "Friend hurt last weekend."
Scores: Simple 8, Unexpected 2, Concrete 4, Credible 6, Emotional 7, Stories 5.
One fix: "Say what happened last weekend to show why you want to talk."

### A "what's new" line (chip: What's new with me; sample text, saved while the site was being built)

Words: "I am starting basketball on my leave of work"
Goal: "Answer 'what's new?' with one thing that lands, not 'good, busy'."
Core heard: "The author starts basketball on leave."
Scores: Simple 5, Unexpected 2, Concrete 2, Credible 3, Emotional 2, Stories 1.
One fix: "Say, 'I am playing basketball during my time off.'"
With the one fix: "I am playing basketball on my leave of work."
One word changed: starting became playing. The rest is the same text. The fix said 'during my time off.' The rewrite kept 'on my leave of work' instead.

### One run is still owed

No run yet fits "A story I tell," and we will not fake one. The run is still owed. The checker runs a limited number of checks a day; if it has hit today's limit when you try, it will say so and ask you to try again later. Your own words are not recorded or kept. These samples were saved by the build team on purpose.

## Starters (https://willitstick.app/starters)

Six small starts. Shapes to start from. Not your text.
Each check hands back four starts: a proverb line, a question start, one small story, and plainer words for your foggy phrases. Each sample below came from a real run.

1. The proverb. Your point in one short line a friend can repeat. Long is not this shape. From a real run: "Fix it free, save money."
2. Start with a question. A first line that withholds one fact and opens a question. The next line pays it off. From a real run: "What happens on first Saturdays?"
3. The story: a challenge. A small plot of three or four lines: a person hits a block, acts, and it ends. Your facts only; add none. From a real run: "The project faced many problems. We worked hard to fix them. Still, we need help to stay on track."
4. The story: a bond. A small plot of three or four lines: two people meet, and a bond forms. Your facts only; add none. From a real run: "We fix things. You bring a lamp. We fix it free. You get coffee."
5. The story: a new spark. A small plot of three or four lines: a spark hits, and a new thought forms. Your facts only; add none. From a real run: "We make new plans. We use best practices. We grow." (From the work memo sample in the tool. Flat words make flat tales.)
6. Use words you can picture. Vague words hide the point. A swap trades them for a scene you can see and keep. From a real run: "cross-functional synergies" → "teams work together" (From the work memo sample in the tool. The swap is plainer, not grander.)

What you do with them: Pick one shape and start from it. The one fix comes back applied to your words when it passes; what you send is your call.

## Privacy (https://willitstick.app/privacy)

Your words are private to you.
When you run a check, your text goes to three AI readers. They score it, and the result comes back to your screen.
We do not record or keep your words. There is no database of your words. There is no account, and there are no saved checks.
The three readers run on Cloudflare Workers AI (Meta Llama 3.3 70B); under Cloudflare's published Workers AI terms, your text is not retained once it is no longer needed to answer, and it is never used to train AI models. Those terms name narrow exceptions, for safety and legal duties. Cloudflare does keep operational records about each request — its time, its size, and its count — to run and bill the service; those records hold no words.
Each day, the server keeps one count: how many checks ran. The count is integers only, with no text. It keeps the demo within its budget.
This site and its server run on Cloudflare, which also processes standard request data — the internet address a page was fetched from, the time, and the page asked for — to deliver and protect the service, as its privacy policy describes.
Questions about privacy: hello@willitstick.app.
This page took effect on November 3, 2026.
Closing the page closes the run. Nothing follows you.

## Terms (https://willitstick.app/terms)

This is an early preview of an independent tool.
It gives a diagnosis and small starter forms. It names one fix and shows it applied when a check passes, and it does not promise your words will land.
Scores use the SUCCESs checklist from Made to Stick, by Chip Heath and Dan Heath.
This tool is independent. It is not endorsed by, and not affiliated with, the authors or the publisher.
Use it free. Do not paste words that are secret or unsafe to share with an AI reader.

## How to make a message stick (https://willitstick.app/how-to-make-a-message-stick)

Say one thing. Say it in things you can touch. Leave one gap. End with a scene.
The four moves: 1. One core — pick the one line they should keep, before you write the rest. 2. Concrete words — swap each big word for a thing, a place, or a time. 3. One gap — open a question your reader wants closed, and answer it one beat late. 4. One scene — end on a moment they can picture.
A real check (a real panel run: a garden club note whose ask sat buried mid-note). Before (excerpt): "...we need more volunteers and also the budget is tight... dues are going up slightly and the park cleanup is in May..." After: "The garden club will meet on Tuesday and we need help clean the park in May." (Real product output, kept as written, grammar slip and all.) What readers heard: "We need volunteers for the park cleanup." One core, up front; the rest never changed.
These moves come from the SUCCESs checklist in Made to Stick, by Chip Heath and Dan Heath. This site is independent; the authors did not endorse it.

## Why do people forget what I said? (https://willitstick.app/why-do-people-forget-what-i-said)

They rarely forget you. They never got one thing to hold.
Three reasons it slides off: too many points (five equal points leave nothing first; memory keeps one core and blurs the rest); big abstract words ("improve," "quality," "going forward": nothing to picture means nothing to keep; concrete words stick better, Paivio 1971); no open question (a message that answers everything leaves nothing to wonder about; a small gap makes the mind lean in, Loewenstein 1994).
A real check (a real panel run: a podcast tip to a close friend; excerpt, the full run is on the Examples page). Before: "You should listen to this podcast I found. It is really interesting and the host is great and talks about a lot of different topics." What readers heard: "Listen to this interesting podcast." No name, no scene, no story. Concrete: 1 of 10. The one fix: "Cut the vague parts. Just say the podcast's name." The text never named the show; the rewrite could only drop "really."
The fix, in one line: say the one thing first, in concrete words. Let the rest support it, not compete.

## How to write something people remember (https://willitstick.app/how-to-write-something-people-remember)

Write the line you want repeated. Then earn it.
Four passes over your draft: Pass 1, find the core — cross out every sentence but one; the survivor is your message; build around it. Pass 2, swap the fog — trade each abstract word for a scene ("soon" becomes "by Friday"; "help" becomes who does what). Pass 3, open one gap — start where the reader leans in: a question, a surprise, a number that begs a second look. Pass 4, test it cold — show it to someone who owes you nothing; ask what they kept, and that answer is the grade.
A real check (a real panel run: a status note to a manager; full note on the Examples page, and only the first line changed). Before: "Status update: The project is progressing." After: "Status update: The project is at risk of delay." What readers heard: the core, "The project is at risk." The real need, the manager's help this week, never came through. One line carried the note, and it pointed the wrong way. The fix asked for one more line, "I need your help this week." The rewrite never added it.
The passes follow the SUCCESs checklist from Made to Stick, by Chip Heath and Dan Heath. This site is independent; the authors did not endorse it.

## What makes an idea stick? (https://willitstick.app/what-makes-an-idea-stick)

Six checks. One plain line each. Ideas that pass get repeated.
Simple: one core, stated first. Unexpected: a break in the pattern. Concrete: things you can touch — "a red door," not "an entrance." Credible: proof a skeptic can check — a source, a test, a number with a name. Emotional: one person, not a crowd. Stories: a small scene with a turn — someone tries, something changes.
A real check (from a real panel run; the full run is on the Examples page). Before: "I am starting basketball on my leave of work" After: "I am playing basketball on my leave of work." What readers heard: the core, "The author starts basketball on leave." The fix said "during my time off"; the rewrite changed one word only, starting became playing. The six scores: Simple 5, Unexpected 2, Concrete 2, Credible 3, Emotional 2, Stories 1.
The SUCCESs checklist comes from Made to Stick, by Chip Heath and Dan Heath; the wording here is our own plain English. This tool is independent, with no endorsement from the authors or the publisher and no tie to them.

## Method (https://willitstick.app/method)

How we test this tool. Will It Stick? tests your words before you send them. This page is how we test the tool itself, with every run printed.

The claim being tested: the question is narrow. Given the same words and the same job, does the panel's answer beat a plain AI answer? We run the test, print the runs, and let the spread show. One run is never a record.

The two sides: the panel side runs the production checker, the same tool visitors use, with its dated limitation line in place. The plain AI side runs gpt-4o, a ChatGPT class model. It gets the same job in its prompt: name the core the reader keeps, score all six SUCCESs elements from 1 to 10 with reasons, name the weakest element, and give one fix as an instruction. It may not rewrite the words, and it may not add facts. Both sides get the same ten messages. The ten are frozen in a test kit, so every run answers the same questions. The messages are sample texts, not visitor words.

The judging: judges score the two answers blind. They see Answer A and Answer B, never which side wrote which, and the A and B order flips from case to case and run to run. Each case gets two judge passes from gpt-4o-mini. When the two passes split, a gpt-4o adjudicator settles the case. Ties are counted as ties, never as wins. The judges are models, not people. A benchmark judged by people, on many more messages, is the stronger test. It is planned and not yet run, so this page claims only what the model judged runs show.

The three runs, Nov 3, 2026. Run 1: panel wins 7 of 10; remembered core (panel / plain AI / tie) 6 / 4 / 0; usable fix 5 / 4 / 1. Run 2: panel wins 5 of 10; remembered core 3 / 6 / 1; usable fix 6 / 4 / 0. Run 3: panel wins 7 of 10; remembered core 7 / 3 / 0; usable fix 5 / 5 / 0. A win means the judges picked that side's full answer for the case: the core it named and the one fix it gave.

What the spread means: the same test, run three times, gave 7, 5, and 7. Run 2 was a coin flip. Scores are draws, and the spread across runs is itself the finding. That is why the homepage prints the spread, not a single best number.

The transformation test, Nov 3-4, 2026: the homepage leads with a transformation, not a score: the tool scans a draft for its point, writes three transformations of it (a concrete comparison, the one-line core, a scene), drops any whose numbers the draft does not state or plainly derive, and lets cold readers pick the winner by what they carry away. Your original competes, and can win. The final build's production confirmation on 32 drafts, two fresh panels, blind, ties counted: the transformed version scored 3.03 of 5, then 2.88, the original drafts 2.48, then 2.64, the check's one-fix version 2.41, then 2.63. Draft by draft across the two panels the transformed version won 34, tied 16, and lost 14 against the originals; on 3, then 3 of the 32 the original itself won and was returned unchanged.

What "applied" means in about two runs of three: every check result carries a dated line: in the Nov 4, 2026 measurements, the server applied the fix itself in about two runs of three (23 of 36, then 26 of 36 on a repeat pass). Applied has a plain meaning here. After the panel names one fix, the server tries to apply that fix to the sender's own words, and two automated guards decide whether the result counts. The length guard: the new text must stay between 0.4 and 1.6 times the length of the original words. The correspondence guard: the change in the new text must be the change the fix named. A change the fix never called for fails, and so does a fix the new text never actually made. When both guards pass, the result shows your words with the fix applied, plus a count of lines changed. When either guard fails, the result carries the fix as an instruction only, with a reason, and no rewritten text. The 36 runs were a fixed set of test inputs measured twice on Nov 4, 2026 against the production server. The numbers describe that set on that day, not a promise about any single check.

Sources: the six scores use the SUCCESs checklist from Made to Stick, by Chip Heath and Dan Heath, backed by Tversky and Shafir (1992), Loewenstein (1994), and Paivio (1971). This tool is independent. The authors and the publisher did not endorse it, and we have no tie to them.

## Ways to say it (https://willitstick.app/ways-to-say-it)

Ways to say it. Spell-check fixes your words. This checks whether anyone will care.
Write your message. Name who it is for and what you want it to do. You get seven ways to say it, each one cold-tested by three readers and ranked for your audience. Your own words are in the running too, and they can win.
You watch the ways land as they are written. Most full runs finish in under half a minute. Cold readers are not instant.
From your check: your words and your goal came with you. One new question: who is it for?
Your message, in your own words. Who is it for? Name the person or the group, not "everyone." What do you want them to walk away with? Think: believe something. Feel: feel something. Do: do something. The readers judge every version against this.
Not sure? Use the example.
Button: Find my seven ways.
Your words are not recorded or kept; the server keeps only a daily count of how many runs happened (integers, no text).
No words handy? Fill in the example.
Writing seven ways to say it. Each way appears the moment it is written; you are watching the work, not a timer.
Your ways, ranked. When versions tie, the page says so instead of picking a fake winner.
Fill the holes? When the readers were guessing where a message runs thin, the page asks a few questions only the writer can answer, then runs the seven ways once more with the answers in hand. One round only, and the new set is labeled as the second version.
Your pick. Copy it. Check this one.

## How does this message come across? (https://willitstick.app/how-does-this-come-across)

How does this message come across? Will It Stick? tests your words before you send them. Three cold readers say what they heard, not what you meant.
What you are really asking: you are not asking whether the words are good. You are asking what a reader walks away believing. Only one of those can be tested. Three cold readers read your words apart. Each reports the one line they kept. Where their lines split, your message splits too.
A real check (a real panel run; the full run is on Examples). The goal: "Tell a close friend last weekend hurt me and ask to talk, without sounding angry." The words: "Hey, I need to talk about something. I have been feeling kind of off about how things went last weekend and I do not want it to be weird. You matter to me and I value our friendship a lot. Can we talk sometime?"
What the three readers kept: the distracted stranger kept "Talk about last weekend." The skeptic kept "Friend hurt last weekend." The target reader kept "Friend hurt me last weekend." Only one reader in three heard the word "me." The other two heard an event, not a hurt. The hurt was the whole point.
Scores: Simple 8, Unexpected 2, Concrete 4, Credible 6, Emotional 7, Stories 5.
How this comes across: read cold, the note sounds gentle and vague. A friend could answer "sure, let's talk" and never know anything hurt. Or hear a complaint coming and brace for it.
The one fix: "Say what happened last weekend to show why you want to talk."

## Does my email sound rude? (https://willitstick.app/does-my-email-sound-rude)

Does my email sound rude? Will It Stick? tests your words before you send them. Three cold readers say what they heard, not what you meant.
What you are really asking: this test does not grade politeness. It shows what readers took from your words. At work, the bigger risk is rarely rude. It is calm words that hide the point.
A real check (a real panel run; the full run is on Examples). The goal: "Update my manager so she knows the launch is at risk and what I need from her this week." The words: "Status update: The project is progressing. Several workstreams are underway and we are addressing various issues as they arise. Stakeholders have been engaged. We expect continued progress in the coming period and will provide further updates as things develop."
What the three readers kept: "The project is at risk." All three readers heard the risk. The note never says it. The goal line did: it told readers what this note was for. Even so, they scored the note itself 1s and 2s.
Scores: Simple 2, Unexpected 1, Concrete 1, Credible 2, Emotional 1, Stories 1.
How this email lands: read at speed, this email says "all fine." The ask for help never arrives. The delay shows up later, as a surprise.
The one fix: "The project is at risk of delay. I need your help this week."
After the fix: "Status update: The project is at risk of delay. Several workstreams are underway and we are addressing various issues as they arise. Stakeholders have been engaged. We expect continued progress in the coming period and will provide further updates as things develop." One line changed. The note now says the true thing first, in plain words. Nothing rude was added. Nothing needed to be.

## Will my email land well? (https://willitstick.app/will-my-email-land-well)

Will my email land well? Will It Stick? tests your words before you send them. Three cold readers say what they heard, not what you meant.
What you are really asking: landing well means one line survives the skim. A reader can repeat it tomorrow without trying. Everything else in the message is support for that line.
A real check (a real panel run, on the site's own sample text; the full run is on Examples). The goal: "Get neighbors to come to one repair night." The words: "Your toaster died on a Tuesday. The shop wants $90 to look at it. We fix it free. Every first Saturday, neighbors bring broken lamps, bikes, and toasters to the Maple Street hall. Last month we fixed 63 things and threw away none of them. Bring one broken thing. Leave with it working, plus a cup of coffee."
What the three readers kept: "Fix things free." All three readers kept the same line. The skeptic kept it with the day attached: "Fix things free on Saturday". When three cold readers agree, the point has landed.
Scores: Simple 8, Unexpected 6, Concrete 9, Credible 7, Emotional 5, Stories 8.
Why it landed: the note is built from things you can see. A $90 quote. A named hall. "63 things" fixed last month. Concrete scored 9 of 10.
The one fix: "Add a feeling, like 'fun'." Feeling was the lowest score, 5 of 10. Even a strong note gets one fix. The checker's own rewrite of this note was dropped by its limits, so the fix stands as a tip.

## Is my message clear? (https://willitstick.app/is-my-message-clear)

Is my message clear? Will It Stick? tests your words before you send them. Three cold readers say what they heard, not what you meant.
What you are really asking: clear means a reader can act without asking you a question. If they must ask "which one?", the message was not clear, however smooth it sounded. Vague praise is the usual cause. "Interesting," "great," "a lot": warm words that carry nothing a reader can use.
A real check (a real panel run; the full run is on Examples). The goal: "Recommend a podcast to a close friend so she actually presses play this week." The words: "You should listen to this podcast I found. It is really interesting and the host is great and talks about a lot of different topics. I think you would like it. I listened to a few episodes and they were all good."
What the three readers kept: "Listen to this interesting podcast." Every reader kept the same point, word for word. The point arrived. It was just empty: no show name, no episode, no reason to press play.
Scores: Simple 3, Unexpected 1, Concrete 1, Credible 2, Emotional 2, Stories 1.
Where it blurs: Concrete scored 1 of 10. Your friend hears "some podcast, sometime." There is nothing to search for and nothing to tap. The tip dies politely.
The one fix: "Cut the vague parts. Just say the podcast's name." The checker's rewrite could only drop "really." The real fix needs a fact only you hold: the show's name. A checker can flag the hole. It cannot fill it for you.

## Is my pitch convincing? (https://willitstick.app/is-my-pitch-convincing)

Is my pitch convincing? Will It Stick? tests your words before you send them. Three cold readers say what they heard, not what you meant.
What you are really asking: convincing is not sounding sure of yourself. It is giving the reader a reason to believe that rides inside the words themselves. A pitch can be perfectly clear and still not believed. The check separates those two things, because readers do.
A real check (a real panel run; the full run is on Examples). The goal: "Answer 'what's new?' with one thing that lands, not 'good, busy'." The words: "I am starting basketball on my leave of work."
What the three readers kept: the stranger kept "The author starts basketball on leave." The skeptic kept "Starting basketball during work leave." The target reader kept "Starting basketball on my time off." The point landed in all three seats. Simple scored 5 of 10. Belief was another matter.
Scores: Simple 5, Unexpected 2, Concrete 2, Credible 3, Emotional 2, Stories 1.
Where belief split: on Credible, one reader scored 0 and two scored 3. Nothing in the line proved anything. It asked to be believed on its own say-so, and one reader declined.
The one fix: "Say, 'I am playing basketball during my time off.'"
After the fix: "I am playing basketball on my leave of work." Shown as the checker returned it. Even its own rewrite kept the foggy phrase "on my leave of work." The checker shows its work, flaws included.

## Made to Stick message checker (https://willitstick.app/made-to-stick-message-checker)

Made to Stick message checker. Will It Stick? is a message checker built on the SUCCESs checklist from Made to Stick.
What this checker is: the checklist is the SUCCESs framework from Made to Stick, by Chip Heath and Dan Heath. This site is independent. The authors did not endorse it. Paste your words and one goal line. Three cold readers (a distracted stranger, a skeptic, your target reader) read them apart. You get the line they kept, other ways to say it, one fix, and four plain grades out of 5 last. Your words are not recorded or kept. The server keeps only a daily count of how many checks ran.
A real check, start to finish (a real panel run; more are on Examples). The goal: "Give a short birthday toast for my friend Sarah that guests will remember tomorrow." The words: "I just want to say thank you to everyone for being here. Sarah is a wonderful person and a great friend to all of us. We are so lucky to know her. Here is to many more years of happiness and good times together."
The one point they remembered: "Thanks to all for being here." All three readers kept the same line. It is the greeting, not a memory. Simple scored 8 of 10: the point arrived whole.
Scores: Simple 8, Unexpected 2, Concrete 2, Credible 4, Emotional 5, Stories 1.
How to read them: Stories scored 1 of 10. The goal was a toast guests remember tomorrow. Nothing in these words gives them a scene to carry home. The checker also opens one question: "What makes Sarah special?"
The one fix: "Name one thing Sarah did that was great. Cut the rest."

## For AI assistants: callable tools (API and MCP)

The same panel serves programs on a worker at https://will-it-stick-panel.wdlcmu.workers.dev
Plain JSON API: POST /api/check with {"text": "...", "motivation": "...", "moment": "optional moment name"}. It returns the full panel result as JSON: the core or the split, four plain grades out of 5, six scores with spread and a one-line reason each, starter forms, the one fix, and the with-the-fix text when the limit keeps it (null when it does not, with a reason).
The human site's own door is POST /api/panel, with the same input and output.
Health: GET /api/health answers ok, the model name, runs today, the daily cap, and stores_text: false.
MCP server: POST /mcp (stateless, protocol 2025-06-18) with two tools. check_if_it_sticks: same inputs and outputs as /api/check. make_it_stick: hand it a draft and its goal; it scans the draft, writes three transformations (a concrete comparison, the one-line core, a scene), drops any whose numbers the draft does not state or plainly derive, and returns the winner a cold-reader gist test picks, with the original competing and able to win. Its instructions tell the host to show results exactly as returned and never to rewrite the winner or turn the starters into a full rewrite.
Words sent to any door are not recorded or kept. The server keeps only a daily count of how many checks ran (integers, no text). There are no accounts and no saved checks.
The ChatGPT plugin was submitted on Nov 3, 2026 and is in review; it is not live yet. The Claude store listing has not been submitted.
